paras: The whipping of Jordan Denny was a night attack on an elderly Black mail carrier at his home in Lancaster, Garrard County, Kentucky, in early November 1881, shortly before his planned wedding. Accounts disagree on the night, the attackers and his injuries, and papers in Kentucky, Texas and Utah all treated it as a comic item.

According to the Lancaster column of the Stanford Interior Journal, Denny was "the old negro" who carried the mail between the post office and the depot, a widower who had courted many women before settling on a woman from Stanford. The out-of-state versions gave his age as sixty and said his daughter opposed the marriage.

In the Interior Journal's telling, his other sweethearts took ropes and switches to his house on the Monday night before the Tuesday wedding. They burst open the door and tried to tie him, but only struck him several times with switches, and a woman in the house was whipped across the face.

A Dallas Daily Herald telegram instead placed the attack on Wednesday night and said a crowd headed by his daughter tied him to his bed and whipped him "unmercifully." The Salt Lake Herald, dating it to the 9th, said several persons, some of them women, including his daughter, tied and flogged him.
The Interior Journal said Denny was "by this time married," while the Salt Lake Herald said he could not marry for some time; no report of arrests appears in the coverage.

The Interior Journal, the only Kentucky report, played the story as a joke on November 11, calling Denny "a flirt" and his bride one of "Stanford's dusky daughters." A day later the Dallas paper named him Jonathan Denny, omitted his race and said he had been "severely kukluxed." On November 16 the Salt Lake Herald called the whipping a daughter's "new but effective method" for ending her father's romance, again without giving his race.

The local correspondent's account, printed first, describes rival sweethearts, a Monday attack and a failed attempt to tie him, while the distant papers describe a daughter-led crowd, a Wednesday attack and a man tied and badly whipped.

reader.title: Whipping of Jordan Denny
bases: A group broke into Denny's house at night and struck him with switches over his planned marriage (A1, A2, A3); no organized band or racial warning is reported, so the record's 'whitecapping' rests only on the Dallas brief's word 'kukluxed' (A2).

A local Kentucky column (A1) and two out-of-state paragraphs (A2, A3) agree that a group whipped the elderly Denny at his home at night just before his wedding, though they disagree on the night, the attackers and the injuries.

accounts.label: Lancaster correspondent
accounts.gist: Rival sweethearts, armed with ropes and switches, broke into Denny's home on the Monday night before his Tuesday wedding, failed to tie him but switched him and a woman present; he married anyway.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: On Wednesday night, the eve of the wedding, a crowd headed by Denny's daughter, who opposed the match, tied him to his bed and whipped him unmercifully, leaving him unfit to marry for some time.

framing.detail: The Interior Journal treated it as a joke, calling Denny 'a flirt' and quoting 'love laughs at locksmiths, ropes and switches'.
The Dallas Daily Herald ran a one-sentence telegram saying Denny was 'severely kukluxed', with no race given.
The Salt Lake Herald framed the whipping as a daughter's 'new but effective method for exterminating the romance' from her father.

conflicts.note: The local column and the Salt Lake paragraph agree on Jordan.
